transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Um… I guess it’s mostly because I’m having trouble making myself make sense. Like in my artist statements, or notes for clients, or even in meetings, I’ll start explaining one thing—like texture or color—and then somehow I’m talking about the budget, or what something secretly means, and people just kind of stare.

They keep saying they can’t follow what I’m trying to explain, which is frustrating because in my head it’s connected. Like, texture and money are connected sometimes, especially with materials, but then I lose the thread and… yeah. That’s why I came in.
Have you been feeling unusually energized lately?

Yeah… I think so. It comes in these bursts where I’ll suddenly take on, like, three proposals at once, and then I’m reorganizing the whole studio because the shelves are “wrong,” and then I’m sketching all night.

And then somehow I’m emailing curators at weird hours and cutting materials for pieces I haven’t even budgeted yet—which is a problem, because materials are so expensive now, especially the good plywood, and I always think I can make it work if the concept is strong enough. But yeah, I guess that is more energized than usual.
Have you been hearing voices when no one else is around?

Sometimes, yeah. Not like a big booming voice or anything. It’s more like when I’m alone in the studio, I’ll hear this woman quietly commenting, like from behind the shelves.

And the shelves are kind of a mess, so at first I think maybe someone came in, or it’s the building making noise, or—well, the studio has weird acoustics because of the concrete and all the wood stacked up. But it feels real enough that I go check, and there’s no one there.

Sometimes it’s not a voice exactly, it’s like I smell hot metal near an unfinished piece, like something’s been heated, but nothing is on. That really bothers me because I start worrying about safety, but then I check and there’s nothing.
Have you been feeling unusually high, euphoric, or irritable lately?

Yeah… I do get that. Like there are stretches where I feel really lit up, almost like everything clicks and I’m unstoppable, and every idea I have feels brilliant—like I can see the whole piece finished before anyone else understands it.

But then, weirdly, if a collaborator makes some small comment, like about changing a material or “maybe simplifying,” I can snap. Not always yelling, but I get sharper than I mean to, and afterward it feels bigger than what they actually said.
During these energized periods, do you need much less sleep than usual?

Yeah, during those times I can sleep, like… two or three hours after working late, and then I wake up weirdly bright, like I’m ready to just keep going.

It’s not like when I pull a normal all-nighter and feel gross and shaky. I’ll get up and start thinking about the piece again, or the layout, or whatever I left unfinished, and I don’t really feel tired the way I usually would.
Have you ever heard that woman’s voice at a time when your mood felt normal—not especially energized, high, or irritable?

Yeah… I think so. There was this quieter stretch, like maybe a month, where I wasn’t all revved up like that. I was sleeping more normally, not feeling like I could do everything at once.

But I still heard her sometimes, those little comments from behind the shelves. And I kept getting… I don’t know, messages isn’t the right word, but I’d look at normal studio stuff—scraps, labels, marks on wood—and feel like there were hidden warnings in them. That went on for a few weeks, even though my mood felt pretty normal.
At any time, have the voice and hidden warnings continued for at least two weeks when you were not feeling especially high, energized, or irritable?

Yeah… yes, I think it did. There was that quieter month where I wasn’t in that “I can do anything” mode, and I was sleeping more normally, not staying up with all the ideas racing.

But the voice was still there sometimes, like little comments from behind the shelves. And I’d still look at regular studio things—labels, scraps, marks in the wood—and feel like they were warning me about something. It wasn’t the whole month every second, but it was going on for several weeks, definitely more than two.
Have you had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

I don’t know if I’d call it depressed most of the day nearly every day… I mean, I’ve had low stretches, sure, where everything felt kind of gray and I didn’t want to deal with people.

But two full weeks like that, most of the day? I’m not really sure. Time gets weird for me when I’m in the studio, because one bad afternoon can feel like three days, and then I’ll get distracted by a project or errands or, like, reorganizing supplies for no reason. So… I can’t say clearly yes to that.
Have there been times when the voice or the hidden warnings lasted while your mood felt normal for most of the day?

Yeah… that’s what I mean about that quieter month. I wasn’t feeling, like, unstoppable or wired, and I was sleeping more normally.

But even then, the voice would still pop up sometimes—comments from behind the shelves—and I’d still look at ordinary studio stuff, like scraps or labels or marks in wood, and feel like there were warnings in them. It went on for several weeks, even when my mood felt mostly normal.
Have you had any seizures?

Seizures? I don’t… I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve had moments where I space out, but I think everyone does that, especially when I’m working on something repetitive. Like sanding or sorting colors, I can lose track of time.

But actual seizures, like what people mean by that—I haven’t noticed anything like that, or no one’s told me I had one.
Have you been using any drugs like cannabis, amphetamines, cocaine, LSD, or other substances around the times these experiences happen?

I mean… not really? I don’t think there’s a pattern like that.

I’m not, like, doing cocaine or LSD or anything. Cannabis… I’ve been around it at parties, but parties are weird because everyone’s talking too loud and the music makes the walls feel busy, so I usually just end up in the kitchen looking at the magnets on the fridge. But I can’t say those experiences happen because of drugs.

I don’t know if caffeine counts, because I drink too much coffee sometimes when I’m working, but that’s not really what you mean, right?
Have you had any head injury where you lost consciousness?

I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve bumped my head before, like normal stuff—cabinet doors, low shelves in the studio, that kind of thing—but not where I blacked out or woke up on the floor or anything.

Unless you mean something really brief? I don’t remember losing consciousness.
During those energized times, do you find yourself much more active than usual?

Yeah, I do. It’s like I suddenly have… a whole engine running.

I’ll take on three proposals at once, and then I’m reorganizing the studio because the shelves “need” to make sense, and then I’m sketching all night. And while I’m doing that I’ll email curators, start cutting materials for pieces I haven’t even budgeted for yet—like, I know that sounds impractical, but in the moment it feels like I can finally see how everything should fit.

The studio gets kind of chaotic, actually. I’ll find scraps from one project mixed with invoices and half-labeled paint tubes, and then I’ll decide I need a better system, and that becomes another whole thing. So… yes, much more active than usual.
Have the voice and the hidden warnings been happening altogether for at least one month?

Yeah… I think so. More than a month, definitely.

It’s hard to pin down because I didn’t write it down at first—I was trying to pretend it was just the studio being weird, like the old pipes and the smell of solvents, and I kept blaming the materials. But the hidden warnings in the textures and the voice, or sometimes those smells in the studio… that’s been going on for, I guess, around eleven months now.

Almost a year, which sounds worse when I say it out loud.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed nearly every day?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, I’ve had stretches where I felt really down or kind of stuck, especially when work wasn’t going well or I’d get behind on applications—those deadlines all pile up and then the studio starts feeling like this accusing place, which sounds dramatic, but—

Sorry. For the two weeks nearly every day part, I don’t know that I can say yes clearly. I’ve had bad periods, but I’m not sure I tracked it that way.
For at least one full month, were the voice or hidden warnings present while you were not feeling especially high, energized, or irritable?

Yes… there was at least one month like that, I think.

It was quieter, not the whole “I can do ten things and never sleep” kind of period. I was sleeping more normally, and I didn’t feel unstoppable or especially wound up. I remember because I was trying to keep a regular studio schedule—though then I got distracted reorganizing old canvas rolls, which isn’t really the point.

But during that time, I still heard comments from behind the shelves sometimes, and I was still seeing warnings in normal materials—like textures or scraps or things that should’ve just been studio stuff. That went on for several weeks even when my mood wasn’t high or irritable.
Have you ever had a period lasting at least one week when you felt unusually high or irritable most of the day, nearly every day?

Yeah… I think so. There are stretches where I feel really lit up, like every idea I have is suddenly the right one, like I can see the whole shape of a project at once and I’m almost unstoppable.

And then—sorry, this is a little embarrassing—but if someone in the studio says one small thing, like a collaborator questions a color choice or asks if I’m sure about a direction, I can snap. Like way bigger than the comment deserves. It’s not just annoyed, it’s like my whole body goes sharp.

I’m not sure I’d always track it as “one week” neatly, because time gets weird when I’m working, but yes, I’ve had periods like that where it’s most of the day, nearly every day for a while.
During one of those energized periods, did that state last at least one full week?

Yes… not every single one was perfectly measured, but those energized, irritable stretches have definitely lasted at least a week. They’ve been happening on and off for, I’d say, about ten months now.

It’s like I’ll have too little sleep and too many projects going, and I don’t realize how long it’s been until the apartment is covered in sketches and half-finished materials. I keep thinking, “I just need one more day,” and then suddenly it’s been more than a week.
Have you had any episodes of losing time or awareness?

I don’t know… not really, I don’t think. I mean, I lose track of time when I’m working, like I’ll start cleaning brushes and then suddenly the light in the room is different, but that feels more like getting absorbed, not like I blacked out.

“Losing awareness” sounds more serious than what I’ve noticed. Unless you mean forgetting why I walked into a room, because I do that constantly, but I think everyone does, right? Especially if there are too many things on the floor or I’m trying to remember where I put the smaller palette knives. So… no, I haven’t noticed episodes like that, I don’t think.
Over the time since these experiences began, have you spent most of that time in a clearly high or irritable mood?

Yeah… I think, looking back, more of the time has been like that than not. Not always at the same volume, if that makes sense—some weeks it’s really obvious, like I’m buzzing and everything irritates me, and other times it’s more just this push underneath everything.

But if I’m honest, the calmer stretches have been shorter. I kept telling myself I was just in a productive phase, or that it was because I had shows to prepare for—though honestly there’s always some reason, some deadline, some thing with the studio space—but across the whole period, I think I’ve spent more of it high-strung and overproductive than actually settled.

I remember because I was trying to keep a regular studio schedule—though then I got distracted reorganizing old canvas rolls, which isn’t really the point.

But during that time, I still heard comments from behind the shelves sometimes, and I was still seeing warnings in normal materials—like textures or scraps or things that should’ve just been studio stuff. That went on for several weeks even when my mood wasn’t high or irritable.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether manic episodes have occurred, to distinguish schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder and bipolar I disorder with psychotic features.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period lasting at least one week when you felt unusually high or irritable most of the day, nearly every day?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: For stretches I feel lit up and almost unstoppable, like every idea is brilliant, but then a small comment from a collaborator can make me snap in a way that feels bigger than the situation.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a sustained period of unusually high or irritable mood, which directly matches elevated or irritable mood.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. There are stretches where I feel really lit up, like every idea I have is suddenly the right one, like I can see the whole shape of a project at once and I’m almost unstoppable.

And then—sorry, this is a little embarrassing—but if someone in the studio says one small thing, like a collaborator questions a color choice or asks if I’m sure about a direction, I can snap. Like way bigger than the comment deserves. It’s not just annoyed, it’s like my whole body goes sharp.

I’m not sure I’d always track it as “one week” neatly, because time gets weird when I’m working, but yes, I’ve had periods like that where it’s most of the day, nearly every day for a while.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a sustained manic episode severe enough to support bipolar I disorder with psychotic features versus schizoaffective or schizophrenia.
doctor.question: During one of those energized periods, did that state last at least one full week?

target_item.name: Manic Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: The energized, irritable stretches with too little sleep and too many projects have been part of my life for about 10 months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of an energized/manic period, specifically whether it lasted at least one full week.

patient.answer:
Yes… not every single one was perfectly measured, but those energized, irritable stretches have definitely lasted at least a week. They’ve been happening on and off for, I’d say, about ten months now.

It’s like I’ll have too little sleep and too many projects going, and I don’t realize how long it’s been until the apartment is covered in sketches and half-finished materials. I keep thinking, “I just need one more day,” and then suddenly it’s been more than a week.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a prominent underlying medical/neurologic cause for the psychosis, especially temporal lobe/organic features that would support F06.2 over a primary psychotic or bipolar-spectrum disorder.
doctor.question: Have you had any episodes of losing time or awareness?

target_item.reason: The question asks about episodes of losing time or awareness, which is not covered by any listed symptom profile. The available profiles describe psychotic symptoms, manic symptoms, duration, and impairment, but not dissociation, blackouts, or impaired awareness episodes.

patient.answer:
I don’t know… not really, I don’t think. I mean, I lose track of time when I’m working, like I’ll start cleaning brushes and then suddenly the light in the room is different, but that feels more like getting absorbed, not like I blacked out.

“Losing awareness” sounds more serious than what I’ve noticed. Unless you mean forgetting why I walked into a room, because I do that constantly, but I think everyone does, right? Especially if there are too many things on the floor or I’m trying to remember where I put the smaller palette knives. So… no, I haven’t noticed episodes like that, I don’t think.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been mood episodes for a substantial portion of the total illness duration, which best distinguishes schizoaffective disorder from schizophrenia now that psychosis outside mood episodes is established.
doctor.question: Over the time since these experiences began, have you spent most of that time in a clearly high or irritable mood?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 2
target_item.manifestation: Looking back over this whole period, the energized, irritable, overproductive stretches have taken up more of the year than the calmer stretches, even when the intensity rises and falls.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the high or irritable mood has occupied most of the time since the experiences began, which directly matches the profile item about manic episode being present for the majority of the illness duration.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think, looking back, more of the time has been like that than not. Not always at the same volume, if that makes sense—some weeks it’s really obvious, like I’m buzzing and everything irritates me, and other times it’s more just this push underneath everything.

But if I’m honest, the calmer stretches have been shorter. I kept telling myself I was just in a productive phase, or that it was because I had shows to prepare for—though honestly there’s always some reason, some deadline, some thing with the studio space—but across the whole period, I think I’ve spent more of it high-strung and overproductive than actually settled.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a clear manic syndrome lasting at least one week with elevated/irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, increased activity, and overinvolvement in projects, along with persistent psychotic symptoms. Crucially, hallucinations and referential/persecutory-type ideas ('hidden warnings') were present for several weeks to at least one month when mood was not high, energized, or irritable, supporting schizoaffective disorder, manic type, over bipolar I disorder with psychotic symptoms. Schizophrenia was considered, but the interview establishes prominent manic episodes for a substantial portion of the illness. Organic psychosis is less likely given denial of seizures, head injury with LOC, or substance linkage.
